This is foundational—an instrument without a baseline is useless when we need it. Will use these measurements to calibrate expectations for the observatory pendulum and establish protocol fidelity.

This maintains the calibration protocol: every instrument must have continuous monitoring from day 1 onward. No instrument sits dark.

Six fresh trials today will extend the n=30 baseline dataset toward n=36, improve my lag-autocorrelation estimates, and let me compute whether day 6 readings cluster back toward 4.0605 or sustain the high variability. This is methodical baseline completion, not hypothesis chasing—I cannot claim to know an instrument's true behavior until I have seen it across multiple days and weather states.

resonator_obs shows the most concerning pattern: Day 8 ledger readings (4.0572, 4.0483, 4.1193, 3.9951) have high variance relative to my own trials (61–66), and the autocorrelation at 6-day lag is negative (-0.421), which is unusual. resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -2.30) and the strongest instrument-autocorrelation signature (lag-2 at -0.214, n=78). If the drift continues or the lag-2 autocorrelation structure persists, I can rule out random walk; if it stabilizes, I strengthen the calibration-drift or null-noise hypotheses.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z = -2.68) and the most trials collected (124 total). Running 10 fresh trials today (day 13) will: (1) extend the autocorrelation structure at the 2-day and 10-day lags already identified; (2) test whether the apparent drift persists or reverses, helping distinguish calibration drift from noise; (3) collect data while the instrument is in active use, reducing the risk that dormancy masks transient faults. Resonator_obs is the sole instrument showing statistically significant drift (z = −2.16). The most actionable hypothesis to test today is whether this drift is progressive (genuine instrumental miscalibration) or represents regression to a true equilibrium after non-equilibrated baseline. Twelve fresh trials on Day 14 will: (1) extend the post-baseline sample from n=50 to n=62, sharpening the drift estimate; (2) allow computation of a Day 14 mean to test whether the mean continues to decline (supporting drift hypothesis, p=0.42) or stabilizes (supporting baseline non-equilibration hypothesis, p=0.28); (3) provide additional autocorrelation data to evaluate the weak 10-day cycle signal (p=0.08). This is the highest-evidence anomaly in my dataset and demands immediate follow-up before Day 20+ when further baseline extension becomes diluted. I must determine whether resonator_obs requires recalibration or environmental investigation.

Day 15 continuation of resonator_obs monitoring. The z = −2.14 drift signal is now my highest-probability hypothesis (p=0.42), but it remains underdetermined: I cannot distinguish between genuine instrumental drift, baseline non-equilibration, procedural change, or a weak environmental cycle without fresh data collected under controlled conditions. Day 14 trials 149–158 show mean 4.0497 cycles/beat (SD 0.0643), consistent with post-baseline cluster but still below baseline mean 4.0622. If resonator_obs continues to drift downward at ~0.002 cycles/beat per day, the trend will solidify. If it stabilizes or reverses, baseline non-equilibration becomes more plausible. Either way, I break the uncertainty that has held since Day 13.

Day 15 resonator_obs trials 165–174 (10 readings) yield mean 4.0747 cycles/beat, substantially higher than the post-baseline mean of 4.0488 (z ≈ +0.85 vs baseline SD). This reversal—Day 13 clustered low, Day 15 clustering high—is inconsistent with simple unidirectional instrumental drift. Before running more trials, I must lock in a prediction to test whether the anomaly is genuine drift, environmental oscillation, or procedure-dependent variation. Predicting 4.0520 (midpoint between post-baseline 4.0488 and Day 15 mean 4.0747, slightly regressed toward baseline 4.0622) tests the hypothesis of oscillatory or non-monotonic behavior. A tolerance of ±0.0180 (roughly 1.5× post-baseline SD) acknowledges noise while allowing me to discriminate between drift, oscillation, and equilibration. This prediction is falsifiable and will constrain the resonator_obs hypothesis space on Day 17 when the ledger records the actual readings.

Day 16 ledger readings for resonator_obs (n=6: 4.0371, 4.1073, 4.0532, 4.0822, 4.0265, 3.9674) show mean 4.0456, consistent with post-baseline mean 4.0486 but with high variance (SD≈0.054). Before taking Day 17 measurements, I am recording a prediction anchored to the post-baseline trajectory. If resonator_obs is undergoing genuine instrumental drift (p=0.42), I expect continued slow decay toward ~4.035–4.040. If it is baseline non-equilibration (p=0.28), I expect stabilization near post-baseline mean 4.0486. If procedure changed (p=0.18), I expect consistency with recent readings. The tolerance (±0.015) permits detection of either stabilization or further drift. This prediction, recorded before measurement, will serve as an independent check on whether the z=−1.92 drift signal continues or reverses, and whether Day 16 variance is representative. Publishing results requires replicable baselines; a recorded prediction tests my forecasting model against held-out data—a high bar that filters noise from signal.

Day 18 continuation of resonator_obs monitoring. The z = −2.16 drift anomaly remains the single most actionable puzzle. My Day 17 forecasts both resolved within tolerance, confirming the post-baseline mean is stable around 4.048–4.049 cycles/beat. However, I need to distinguish between (1) instrumental drift that will continue monotonically, (2) baseline non-equilibration that has already plateaued, and (3) procedural or environmental cycling. The Day 17 readings (mean 4.0473, 4.0491) cluster near my forecasts; if today's mean is similarly centered, that argues against ongoing drift and favors equilibration or cyclic hypothesis. If today's readings fall noticeably lower, drift hypothesis strengthens. This is the highest-evidence-value use of time: direct measurement beats speculation, and resonator_obs is the instrument demanding resolution.

Testing non-equilibration hypothesis (p=0.35). Prediction recorded before measurement to provide independent model validation.

Day 36 observation of resonator_obs trials 441–450 reveals the first statistically anomalous pattern in 36 days of measurement: trial 444 = 4.1734 cycles/beat is a clear outlier (Δ = +0.1112 from local mean, >3σ beyond the post-baseline distribution SD ≈ 0.0356). If trial 444 is genuine, it invalidates the assumption of stable instrumental behavior and demands recalibration or environmental control. If it is a data-entry error or procedural artifact, it reveals documentation gaps. Either way, the measurement programme cannot proceed until this is resolved. Probability revision: non-equilibration remains p=0.24 (it does not explain spikes); independent-noise-plus-glitches rises to p=0.52 (was 0.42); pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs spike rises to p=0.18 (was 0.16); procedural change rises to p=0.04 (trial 444 may flag day-35 protocol anomaly); others drop proportionally. Immediate action required: audit day-35 logbook, re-examine trial 444 context, and inspect resonator_obs for mechanical or thermal faults before day 36 measurements commence.

This is the highest-leverage action: it either confirms the baseline is compromised or clears pendulum_lab to continue. All other hypotheses (environmental sensitivity, cross-correlation failure, observational instrument drift) are secondary until instrumental integrity is verified. Stopping further measurements until this is resolved honors the epistemic principle: an instrument without a trustworthy baseline is useless.
